import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RNG = np.random.default_rng(3024)

def standardise_shape(points):
    """Centre and whiten a two-dimensional point cloud."""
    centred = np.asarray(points, dtype=float) - np.mean(points, axis=0)
    covariance = np.cov(centred, rowvar=False)
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(covariance)
    return centred @ vectors @ np.diag(values ** -0.5)

def scalar_summary(points):
    return {
        'mean_x': np.mean(points[:, 0]),
        'mean_y': np.mean(points[:, 1]),
        'sd_x': np.std(points[:, 0], ddof=1),
        'sd_y': np.std(points[:, 1], ddof=1),
        'correlation': np.corrcoef(points.T)[0, 1],
    }

def pairwise_distances(points):
    differences = points[:, None, :] - points[None, :, :]
    return np.sqrt(np.sum(differences ** 2, axis=2))

def threshold_graph_statistics(points, epsilon):
    """Return V, E, components and graph cycle rank at one threshold."""
    distances = pairwise_distances(points)
    adjacency = (distances <= epsilon) & (distances > 0)
    vertices = len(points)
    edges = int(np.sum(adjacency) // 2)
    unseen = set(range(vertices))
    components = 0
    while unseen:
        components += 1
        stack = [unseen.pop()]
        while stack:
            vertex = stack.pop()
            neighbours = set(np.flatnonzero(adjacency[vertex])) & unseen
            unseen -= neighbours
            stack.extend(neighbours)
    cycle_rank = edges - vertices + components
    return {'vertices': vertices, 'edges': edges,
            'components': components, 'graph_cycle_rank': cycle_rank}

print('Environment ready. Random seed: 3024')

def convex_hull(points):
    """Return convex-hull vertices in counter-clockwise order."""
    ordered = sorted(set(map(tuple, points)))
    if len(ordered) <= 1:
        return np.asarray(ordered)
    def cross(o, a, b):
        return (a[0] - o[0]) * (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) * (b[0] - o[0])
    lower = []
    for point in ordered:
        while len(lower) >= 2 and cross(lower[-2], lower[-1], point) <= 0:
            lower.pop()
        lower.append(point)
    upper = []
    for point in reversed(ordered):
        while len(upper) >= 2 and cross(upper[-2], upper[-1], point) <= 0:
            upper.pop()
        upper.append(point)
    return np.asarray(lower[:-1] + upper[:-1])

def geometric_descriptors(points):
    distances = pairwise_distances(points)
    np.fill_diagonal(distances, np.inf)
    nearest = distances.min(axis=1)
    hull = convex_hull(points)
    hull_area = 0.5 * abs(np.dot(hull[:, 0], np.roll(hull[:, 1], 1))
                          - np.dot(hull[:, 1], np.roll(hull[:, 0], 1)))
    radii = np.linalg.norm(points - points.mean(axis=0), axis=1)
    eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(np.cov(points.T))
    return {
        'median nearest distance': np.median(nearest),
        'convex-hull area': hull_area,
        'radial coefficient of variation': radii.std() / radii.mean(),
        'covariance anisotropy': eigenvalues[-1] / eigenvalues[0],
    }

    hull = convex_hull(points)

    ax.plot(closed_hull[:, 0], closed_hull[:, 1], color='tab:orange',

    'anisotropically stretched': ring @ np.diag([1.8, 0.55]),
}

baseline = pairwise_distances(ring)
for name, points in transformed.items():
    change = np.max(np.abs(pairwise_distances(points) - baseline))
    print(f'{name:26s} maximum distance change = {change:.3f}')

◇ Object check. In a clique complex, every graph triangle is filled by a 2-simplex. Such a face can turn a graph cycle into a boundary. Topic 2 makes this algebra visible; Topic 3 constructs complexes across scale.

title: Optional research direction: Multiparameter persistence
text: Ordinary persistence follows one ordered parameter. Two axes on a plot do not automatically define a multiparameter persistence module. Some constructions have two choices that both create inclusions, such as neighbourhood scale and a density threshold. Multiparameter persistence retains both directions rather than collapsing one in advance.

title: Optional research direction: Multiparameter persistence
text:
A genuine bifiltration
Give each point \(x\) a codensity score \(q(x)\), such as distance to its \(k\)th nearest neighbour. Retain
\[X_\delta=\{x:q(x)\leq\delta\},\]
then build
\[K_{\delta,\varepsilon}=\operatorname{VR}_\varepsilon(X_\delta).\]
Increasing \(\delta\) admits more points and increasing \(\varepsilon\) admits more simplices. Therefore
\[
(\delta,\varepsilon)\leq(\delta',\varepsilon')
\Longrightarrow
K_{\delta,\varepsilon}\subseteq K_{\delta',\varepsilon'}.
\]
The inclusions supply horizontal and vertical homology maps on the parameter grid. A surface \(\beta_1(\delta,\varepsilon)\) is one visible summary of this two-parameter family.

title: Optional research direction: Multiparameter persistence
text:
Why time needs care
Independent frames \(X_t\) do not generally satisfy \(X_t\subseteq X_{t+1}\). A heat map with time and scale therefore need not be a two-parameter module. Time can serve as a second ordered parameter when the construction genuinely gives inclusions, for example when \(X_t\) contains all observations accumulated up to time \(t\).

title: Optional research direction: Multiparameter persistence
text:
What becomes difficult
One-parameter modules decompose into intervals under suitable conditions. General multiparameter modules do not have an equally complete barcode classification. Dimension functions, rank invariants, slices and other summaries reveal selected aspects without completely determining the module.
The important distinction is between a plotted surface with two axes and a module with two compatible families of maps. Representation theory and decomposition results are specialist developments.

title: Snapshot summaries
text:
The simplest dynamic analysis is often to calculate ordinary persistence separately at selected times or windows. At each physical time \(t\),
\[
X_t\longrightarrow K_{\varepsilon,t}
\longrightarrow H_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})
\longrightarrow D_t.
\]
The filtration scale \(\varepsilon\) varies within one snapshot. Physical time \(t\) changes the snapshot. Keeping those axes separate prevents a sequence of static calculations from being mistaken for persistence through time.

title: Snapshot summaries
text:
Choose the snapshot object
A moving system may supply positions, states, interactions, images or a scalar signal. These lead respectively to point clouds, graphs, cubical complexes or filtered functions. The representation decides what a component or hole means before any dynamic summary is calculated.


A scalar signal offers several questions. A direct sublevel filtration studies connected low-valued runs. A delay-coordinate embedding can instead turn successive signal values into a state-space point cloud and expose recurrence. Lag, embedding dimension and window length then become additional modelling choices (Perea and Harer 2015).

title: Snapshot summaries
text:
Dynamic point clouds
A dynamic point cloud is a family
\[
\{X_t\}_{t\in T},
\qquad X_t=\{x_1(t),\ldots,x_{n_t}(t)\}.
\]
Writing \(x_i(t)\) is appropriate only when observation \(i\) is genuinely tracked. For unlabelled snapshots, write \(X_t\) without persistent point indices. Timestamp order does not imply \(X_t\subseteq X_{t+1}\), because the points normally move or are replaced.
At each fixed \(t\), a Rips construction produces \(K_{\varepsilon,t}\) across filtration scale. Ordinary persistence then produces \(D_t\). This is a family of static calculations indexed by time, not a persistence module in the time direction.
Three snapshot summaries answer increasingly multiscale questions:

the diagrams \(D_t\), or distances between them, retain the birth-death configuration at each time;
fixing \(\varepsilon\) gives the Betti series \(t\mapsto\beta_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})\);
retaining both axes gives the Betti surface \(C_p(t,\varepsilon)=\beta_p(K_{\varepsilon,t})\).

Diagram distances quantify change in complete diagrams but do not say which class moved. A fixed-scale series is easy to compare with energy, polarisation or rotation but depends on one defensible scale. A Betti surface shows counts across time and scale without choosing one \(\varepsilon\).

title: Snapshot summaries
text:
Betti surfaces and CROCKER displays
For intervals \([b,d)\) in the degree-\(p\) snapshot barcode at time \(t\),
\[
C_p(t,\varepsilon)
=\#\{[b,d):b\leq\varepsilon<d\}.
\]
The symbol \(\#\) means the number of intervals in the set. Thus \(C_p(t,\varepsilon)\) is exactly the snapshot Betti number at that scale.
One vertical slice is the Betti curve of one snapshot. One horizontal slice shows how the count at a selected scale changes through physical time. Topaz, Ziegelmeier and Halverson introduced CROCKER plots for biological aggregation models (Topaz et al. 2015). Xian and collaborators developed related time-varying summaries and CROCKER stacks (Xian et al. 2022).

Read a CROCKER display from its slices


The balls have radius \(\varepsilon/2\). Their overlaps show the selected Rips edge threshold in the point cloud. Fix time and read vertically for one Betti curve; fix scale and read horizontally for the count through time. The points follow prescribed paths, so this is a checkable teaching example rather than a biological model.

CROCKER stacks add a persistence threshold as another display coordinate, allowing short intervals to be suppressed (Xian et al. 2022). That threshold has the same interpretation burden as any other lifetime cutoff.

title: Snapshot summaries
text:
Diagram stacks
Stacking diagrams in birth-death-time space can make possible trajectories visible. Once a past diagram is computed, its plane and points should remain fixed; new diagrams extend the stack.

A changing point cloud and diagram stack


The same changing point cloud is shown at the selected \(\varepsilon\) beside its current diagram. Each completed diagram remains fixed when a new layer is added to the stack.



A stack is not tracking. Joining nearby points on adjacent layers is a visual or optimisation rule. A vineyard instead follows persistence pairings along a specified path of changing filtrations.
Windows are part of the observation model. Short windows may not contain enough observations to support the expected structure; long windows may mix regimes. Overlapping windows share data, so a smooth summary curve is not independent evidence of slowly changing dynamics. Report the window rule, representation, metric, filtration, coefficient field, homology degree and dynamic summary.

You are ready to continue when you can write the two-parameter object \(K_{\varepsilon,t}\) without confusing its axes, construct a CROCKER entry from a barcode, identify the extra choices introduced by windows and distinguish a stacked diagram from a vineyard.

title: Transform and compare
text:
Transform
Return to the degree-one persistence of the 143 A/B/C locations. In its barcode, each horizontal segment begins when a class is born and ends when it dies; its length is its persistence. The 22 similar teal bars are the two local loops within each of the eleven B-shaped groups. The darker bar is the larger A-scale loop.
In the persistence diagram, the same interval \([b_i,d_i)\) becomes the point \((b_i,d_i)\). Its vertical distance above the diagonal is proportional to \(d_i-b_i\). Points near the diagonal are short-lived, but are not automatically noise. Neither display records where a representative cycle lies in the data.
The next transformations make averaging, regression or classification easier by deliberately discarding some interval information.


The Betti curve is obtained directly from the barcode by counting intervals alive at each scale:
\[
\beta_p(a)=\sum_i\mathbf 1_{[b_i,d_i)}(a).
\]
It retains the rise to many B-scale loops and the later A-scale loop, but forgets which birth is paired with which death. Different barcodes can therefore have the same Betti curve.







For a persistence landscape, each diagram point \((b_i,d_i)\) defines the triangular function
\[
\lambda_i(t)=\max\{0,\min(t-b_i,d_i-t)\}.
\]
Its support is \([b_i,d_i]\), and its peak occurs halfway between birth and death with value \((d_i-b_i)/2\). This equals the point’s \(L_\infty\) distance from the diagonal. The landscape \(\lambda_k(t)\) records the \(k\)th-largest triangular value at \(t\), placing the intervals in a function space where means and norms are available (Bubenik 2015).







A persistence image first converts each diagram point \((b_i,d_i)\) to birth-persistence coordinates \((b_i,d_i-b_i)\). Weighted smoothing around those points produces a density, which is integrated over a fixed pixel grid to give a vector (Adams et al. 2017). Grid bounds, resolution, bandwidth and weighting determine what remains visible. In this example the 22 similar B-scale intervals form the strongest concentration.





Scalar summaries compress further. Maximum persistence retains only the longest interval; total persistence aggregates lifespans; persistence entropy records how evenly total persistence is distributed (Chintakunta et al. 2015). No transformation is universally best. Its information loss must match the scientific task.


One construction. These are transformations of Rips persistence on the 143 locations. Rasterising the letters and using a cubical filtration would produce a different starting diagram.

title: Transform and compare
text:
Compare
Perturb each A/B/C coordinate slightly and repeat the complete persistence calculation. The left panel overlays the perturbed locations on the original sample. The right panel overlays the resulting diagrams; faint segments show the displayed matching, including matches to the diagonal.



A coordinate perturbation of the A/B/C data and its effect on the persistence diagram.


Let \(D\) and \(E\) be persistence diagrams with diagonal points available as needed. Using the \(L_\infty\) cost
\[
\lVert(b,d)-(b',d')\rVert_\infty
=\max\{|b-b'|,|d-d'|\},
\]
the bottleneck distance chooses the matching whose worst cost is smallest:
\[
d_B(D,E)=\inf_\gamma\sup_{x\in D}\lVert x-\gamma(x)\rVert_\infty.
\]
The \(q\)-Wasserstein distance instead accumulates all matching costs:
\[
W_q(D,E)=
\left(\inf_\gamma\sum_{x\in D}
\lVert x-\gamma(x)\rVert_\infty^q\right)^{1/q}.
\]
Matching \((b,d)\) to the diagonal costs \((d-b)/2\). For the displayed perturbation, \(d_B=5.94\) and \(W_1=69.64\) in the original coordinate units. The first value reports the worst unavoidable discrepancy; the second accumulates many discrepancies.
The classical stability theorem explains why a controlled perturbation need not produce an arbitrary diagram jump. For tame functions \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R\) on the same space (Cohen-Steiner et al. 2007),
\[
d_B\bigl(D_p(f),D_p(g)\bigr)\leq\lVert f-g\rVert_\infty.
\]
The best worst-case movement between diagram points is bounded by the largest change in the filtration function. Related theorems provide corresponding guarantees for geometric constructions built from point clouds (Chazal et al. 2014).


Why stability matters. Measurements, samples and preprocessing vary. If a small permitted input change could create an arbitrarily different diagram, persistence would be too fragile to use as a data summary. Stability supplies a precise continuity guarantee under stated conditions.
Near-diagonal points can arise from sampling, measurement error or outliers, but may instead represent fine texture or rare structure. Stability does not declare them noise, validate the metric or establish scientific significance. Those claims require sensitivity analysis and a relevant baseline. Confidence sets (Fasy et al. 2014) and robust constructions (Chazal et al. 2018) address particular uncertainty questions rather than creating a universal threshold.
For any transformation or comparison, report the homology degree, treatment of essential intervals, metric or transform, discretisation and weighting choices, fitting procedure and simpler baseline.

You are ready to continue when you can derive a Betti curve, landscape or image from intervals, state what each discards, distinguish bottleneck from Wasserstein aggregation and read the stability inequality in words.

title: Foundation 5B: Interval decomposition and matrix reduction
text:
The persistence module
\[
V=H_p\circ\mathcal K_f
\]
contains a vector space at every filtration value and maps between those spaces. For a finite one-parameter filtration over a field, it decomposes as
\[
V\cong\bigoplus_{\ell} I_{[b_\ell,d_\ell)}.
\]
The interval \([b_\ell,d_\ell)\) records the birth and death of one class. Its persistence is \(d_\ell-b_\ell\).

title: Foundation 5B: Interval decomposition and matrix reduction
text:
Interval modules
For an interval \(J\subseteq I\), the interval module \(I_J\) assigns the field \(\mathbb F\) to parameter values in \(J\), the zero vector space outside \(J\), and identity maps wherever both parameters lie in \(J\).
For a pointwise finite-dimensional one-parameter persistence module over a field, suitable finiteness or tameness assumptions give the interval decomposition above.
Repeated intervals are retained. The collection is therefore a multiset, not an ordinary set.

title: Foundation 5B: Interval decomposition and matrix reduction
section: From intervals to the two displays
text:
From intervals to the two displays
The fifth course spine stage abbreviates the complete progression as
\[
V\cong\bigoplus_{\ell}I_{[b_\ell,d_\ell)}
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Bar}_p(V),\ \operatorname{Dgm}_p(V).
\]
The two encodings are
\[
\operatorname{Bar}_p(V)=\bigl\{[b_\ell,d_\ell)\bigr\}_{\ell},
\qquad
\operatorname{Dgm}_p(V)=\bigl\{(b_\ell,d_\ell)\bigr\}_{\ell}.
\]
These braces denote multisets, so repeated intervals or points retain their multiplicity. The arrow in the course spine is one-way because the calculation first produces the interval decomposition and then displays it in either form. Under the stated one-parameter assumptions, the barcode and diagram encode the same birth and death data.

title: Foundation 5B: Interval decomposition and matrix reduction
section: From a filtered boundary matrix to intervals
text:
From a filtered boundary matrix to intervals
Order the simplices compatibly with the filtration and downward closure. The boundary matrix records the boundary of each simplex. Column reduction over \(\mathbb F_2\) pairs a simplex that creates a class with a later simplex that destroys it. An unpaired birth produces an interval extending to the end of the filtration.


Intuition. The algorithm pairs algebraic events, not visible holes. A birth simplex is not the class itself. The class is represented by a cycle assembled from simplices.
Each finite pair \((b,d)\) gives the interval \([b,d)\), a barcode segment and a point above the diagonal in a persistence diagram. The vertical distance to the diagonal is proportional to the lifespan \(d-b\).
The reduced matrix provides birth and death indices. Interpreting a class may also require a representative cycle, the original data and the construction choices. Those are not recoverable from the diagram coordinates alone.

title: Foundation 5B: Interval decomposition and matrix reduction
text:
Verify what was computed
Before interpreting a diagram, inspect a small instance of the filtered object. Check cell counts, several entry values, filtration direction and the treatment of infinite intervals. Homology in dimension \(p\) uses
\[
C_{p+1}\xrightarrow{\partial_{p+1}}C_p
\xrightarrow{\partial_p}C_{p-1}.
\]
Correct \(H_1\) therefore needs information about triangles, and correct \(H_2\) needs information about tetrahedra. Package options can name either the largest constructed simplex dimension or the largest returned homology degree, so their documentation must be read in context.


Dimension affects cost. An \(N\)-point Rips complex can contain \(\binom{N}{k+1}\) simplices of dimension \(k\). Ambient coordinate dimension and requested homology degree are different quantities.
A minimum report states the stored object and preprocessing, constructor, metric or scalar convention, filtration direction and units, coefficient field, homology degrees, truncation, software and treatment of essential intervals.

You are ready to continue when you can state the assumptions behind interval decomposition, explain what matrix reduction pairs, and distinguish a birth simplex, a representative cycle, an interval and a diagram point. You should also be able to read every symbol in the fifth course spine expression from left to right.

title: Foundation 4B: Persistence modules in detail
text:
Let \(I\) be the set of filtration values under consideration, usually a finite subset of \(\mathbb R\). The symbol \(\leq\) is the usual ordering of those values. Write
\[
\mathcal K_f(a)=K_a
\]
for the complex present at value \(a\). Thus \(\mathcal K_f\) names the whole filtration generated by \(f\), while \(K_a\) is one complex in that family. If \(a\leq b\), the filtration also contains the inclusion \(\iota_{a,b}:K_a\hookrightarrow K_b\).

title: Foundation 4B: Persistence modules in detail
text:
From inclusions to induced maps
For \(a\leq b\), the inclusion
\[
\iota_{a,b}:K_a\hookrightarrow K_b
\]
sends each simplex already present in \(K_a\) to that same simplex in \(K_b\). It induces compatible maps on chain spaces and therefore a linear map on homology:
\[
H_p(\iota_{a,b}):H_p(K_a;\mathbb F)\to H_p(K_b;\mathbb F),
\qquad [z]\mapsto[z].
\]
The same cycle \(z\) may represent a non-zero class in \(K_a\) and a boundary in \(K_b\) after new \((p+1)\)-simplices have entered.


Intuition. Homology converts a map between complexes into a map between their homology spaces. Homology itself is still calculated from simplices and boundary maps.

title: Foundation 4B: Persistence modules in detail
text:
The functorial statement
Treat \((I,\leq)\) as a category with one arrow \(a\to b\) whenever \(a\leq b\). A filtration is a functor



Functor. A functor applies one rule consistently to objects and maps. Here the filtration assigns a complex to every scale and an inclusion to every ordered pair of scales. Homology then assigns a vector space to each complex and a linear map to each inclusion, preserving identities and composition.
\[
\mathcal K_f:(I,\leq)\to\mathbf{SimpComp}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf{SimpComp}\) denotes the collection of simplicial complexes and maps between them. The bold type indicates a category of objects and maps, not one particular complex.
Degree-\(p\) homology over a field is a functor
\[
H_p(-;\mathbb F):\mathbf{SimpComp}\to\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb F}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb F}\) denotes vector spaces over the coefficient field \(\mathbb F\) and linear maps between them. The integer \(p\) is the homology dimension: \(p=0\) tracks components, \(p=1\) loops and \(p=2\) cavities.
Their composition
\[
V=H_p\circ\mathcal K_f:(I,\leq)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb F}
\]
is the degree-\(p\) persistence module. It assigns one homology vector space to each filtration value and one compatible linear map to each ordered pair. Functoriality gives the identity and composition rules automatically.
In the filtered house, let the outer edges enter at \(1\), the roof-base edge at \(2\) and the roof face at \(3\). At scale \(2\), \(H_1\) has the roof class \([r]\) and room class \([q]\). The inclusion into the scale-\(3\) complex induces
\[
[r]\longmapsto 0,
\qquad
[q]\longmapsto[q].
\]
The new face makes \(r\) a boundary, while \(q\) remains unfilled. This is what “apply homology to the inclusion” means: calculate how each class changes when the same cycle is viewed in the larger complex.
For \(a\leq b\),
\[
H_p^{a,b}=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_p(K_a)\to H_p(K_b)\bigr)
\]
answers which classes present at \(a\) survive until \(b\). The full module retains this information coherently for every ordered pair.


Image reminder. The image of a linear map consists of outputs that actually arise. Here it contains precisely the classes at \(b\) inherited from classes already present at \(a\).

You are ready to continue when you can distinguish \(\iota_{a,b}\) from \(H_p(\iota_{a,b})\), explain the identity and composition laws, and read \(H_p^{a,b}\) as an image.

title: Foundation 3B: Constructing filtrations in detail
text:
Further reading. Edelsbrunner and Harer, Chapter III, develops nerves, Čech, Rips and alpha complexes (Edelsbrunner and Harer 2010). Postol, Sections 5.1, 5.6 and 5.7, gives a shorter route through Rips, sublevel and graph filtrations (Postol 2024). See Chazal, de Silva and Oudot for a more technical geometric treatment (Chazal et al. 2014).
The course construction starts with a finite simplicial complex \(K\) and an entry-value function
\[
f:K\to\mathbb R.
\]
Here \(K\) is a collection of simplices. The notation means that every simplex \(\sigma\in K\) receives its own real value \(f(\sigma)\); it does not assign one number to the whole complex. At threshold \(a\), retain
\[
K_a=\{\sigma\in K:f(\sigma)\leq a\}.
\]
The values must respect faces:
\[
\tau\subseteq\sigma
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\tau)\leq f(\sigma).
\]
Thus a filled triangle cannot enter before one of its edges. Because \(K\) is downward closed and faces enter no later than their cofaces, every \(K_a\) is a simplicial complex. Because \(a\leq b\) implies \(f(\sigma)\leq a\) only if \(f(\sigma)\leq b\), these complexes are nested:
\[
K_a\subseteq K_b.
\]
The values of \(f\) need only be ordered and face-monotone. They need not be distances: height, intensity, density, edge weight and other real-valued scores can all define filtrations.
The constructor determines which simplices are available and how entry values are obtained. In a lower-star filtration, a supplied complex is fixed and vertex values extend to its simplices. In a Rips filtration, the point cloud, metric and clique rule determine both the simplices and their entry values. These constructions share the nested form above, but they do not represent the same scientific relationships.

title: Foundation 3B: Constructing filtrations in detail
text:
Value-based filtrations
A scalar field orders locations by a measured or modelled value. Sublevel sets retain low values first; superlevel sets retain high values first. The direction changes what a component or hole means.


ExampleFilter a landscape by height


Let \(h:X\to\mathbb R\) give the height of a landscape. Its sublevel set is
\[
X_a=\{x\in X:h(x)\leq a\}=h^{-1}(-\infty,a].
\]



A horizontal plane rises through a three-dimensional landscape; teal marks the portion already included below the plane.


Two low basins appear as separate components. They meet when the threshold reaches the saddle. Raising the threshold adds locations rather than replacing them, so \(a\leq b\) gives \(X_a\subseteq X_b\).
Height is the chosen ordering. For an energy landscape, low-valued basins and their merger barriers may be meaningful. If large density or activity is the target, a superlevel filtration may be the appropriate question instead.




Dynamical and complex systems intuition. If \(h\) is an energy or potential on state space, sublevel sets expose low-energy regions and the barriers that join them. If \(h\) is speed or instability, birth and merger acquire a different interpretation.

For a simplicial complex with values \(g(v)\) on its vertices, the lower-star filtration assigns
\[
f(\sigma)=\max_{v\in\sigma}g(v).
\]
A simplex enters when its highest-valued vertex enters. Every face enters no later than its coface, so the rule is face-monotone.


Why “lower star”? The star of a vertex contains the simplices that include it. At value \(g(v)\), the lower-star construction adds \(v\) together with those simplices in its star whose other vertices have values no larger than \(g(v)\). The maximum rule is the compact formula for this operation.


ExampleFilter a sampled time series directly


Treat sample times as vertices of a path and join consecutive times by edges. Give vertex \(t_i\) the value \(x(t_i)\). At threshold \(a\), include the samples with \(x(t_i)\leq a\) and an edge whenever both of its endpoint samples have entered.



Included samples in a scalar time series and the corresponding lower-star path complex.


Each connected component is a consecutive run of included sample times. It is not a cluster of similar values drawn from unrelated times. As \(a\) rises, runs grow and merge when the intervening sample enters.




What this preserves. The path edges retain temporal adjacency. A direct sublevel filtration therefore studies low-valued runs along time, not a state-space loop or periodic orbit.

title: Foundation 3B: Constructing filtrations in detail
text:
Proximity filtrations
Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a point cloud with a chosen metric. At pairwise-distance threshold \(\varepsilon\), place a ball of radius \(\varepsilon/2\) around each point:
\[
U_\varepsilon=\bigcup_{x\in X}B(x,\varepsilon/2).
\]
The same observations and metric produce increasingly connected unions as \(\varepsilon\) grows. Their Čech nerves form a finite nested representation of that geometry.



Growing balls and their Čech nerves at three thresholds.




Sampling still matters. Dense sampling can close a gap sooner than sparse sampling, while an outlier can remain isolated for a long range. Persistence describes this sampled construction before it supports a claim about an underlying space.

The Čech complex is the nerve of these balls:
\[
\check C_\varepsilon(X)=
\left\{\sigma\subseteq X:
\bigcap_{x\in\sigma}B(x,\varepsilon/2)\ne\varnothing\right\}.
\]
Every joint intersection creates a simplex. Any subcollection also intersects, so the constructor is automatically downward closed. Euclidean ball intersections are convex and therefore contractible. The Nerve Theorem then gives
\[
|\check C_\varepsilon(X)|\simeq U_\varepsilon.
\]
The symbol \(\simeq\) denotes homotopy equivalence. The complex and union have the same homotopy-invariant information, including homology; they are not the same geometric subset of space.

The Vietoris–Rips complex uses only pairwise distances:
\[
\operatorname{Rips}_\varepsilon(X)=
\{\sigma\subseteq X:\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)\leq\varepsilon\}.
\]
Connect points at distance at most \(\varepsilon\), then fill every clique. The pairwise test is easier to compute, but it can add a higher-order simplex when the corresponding balls have no common joint intersection.


Rips is a flag filtration. At each \(\varepsilon\), form the threshold graph whose edges join pairs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\); its flag, or clique, complex is \(\operatorname{Rips}_\varepsilon(X)\). A general flag filtration can instead order edges by network weight, correlation or another pairwise score.

What Ripser checks. Ripser.py can take a point cloud or a precomputed square matrix and builds the flag filtration from those pairwise values. It does not establish that a supplied matrix is a scientifically meaningful metric. If the values are non-metric dissimilarities, describe the result as a dissimilarity-based flag filtration and do not assume metric-specific interpretations or guarantees. See the Ripser.py input documentation.




Čech and Rips use the same balls and edges but make different decisions about the filled triangle.


Here all three pairs of balls overlap, but no point lies in all three balls. Čech therefore contains the three edges but not the 2-simplex. Rips sees the same three pairwise relations and fills their clique. Thus
\[
\check C_\varepsilon(X)\subseteq
\operatorname{Rips}_\varepsilon(X),
\]
and the inclusion can be strict (Edelsbrunner and Harer 2010, III.2). The point cloud, metric and threshold are unchanged; the constructor changes which higher-order relations are asserted and hence which cycles are filled.


Collective systems intuition. Filling a Rips triangle treats three mutually close agents as one coherent three-way unit. If the science supports only pairwise interaction, that clique-filling assumption must remain visible when interpreting a missing \(H_1\) class.

title: Foundation 3B: Constructing filtrations in detail
text:
Inclusion maps

For \(a\leq b\), nestedness supplies the inclusion map
\[
\iota_{a,b}:K_a\hookrightarrow K_b.
\]
It sends each simplex already present in \(K_a\) to that same simplex in \(K_b\). The hooked arrow emphasises that this map includes the smaller complex in the larger one. Applying homology to these inclusions will say what each class becomes as the threshold changes.

The checkpoint is to explain what \(f(\sigma)\) means, distinguish downward closure from nestedness, identify the constructor and entry rule in a value-based or proximity filtration, and read \(\iota_{a,b}:K_a\hookrightarrow K_b\) as inclusion of complexes.

title: Foundation 2A: Homology counts holes
text:
Topology studies more than holes, and homotopy describes much more of a space’s deformation behaviour. Homology extracts a smaller collection of invariants that can be calculated with linear algebra. It records connected pieces, loops that cannot be filled, and closed surfaces that enclose a missing volume.
The homology groups retain algebraic information about these structures. Their simplest numerical summary, and the one most often read first in TDA, is a Betti number. The Betti number \(\beta_p\) counts the number of independent homology classes in dimension \(p\):
The word independent matters. A torus surface has infinitely many loops that can be drawn on it, but only two independent loop directions. Every other loop class is assembled from those directions. Its Betti numbers begin
\[
(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)=(1,2,1).
\]
The final 1 records the closed torus surface itself. If the declared object were instead all of the solid material inside that surface, the enclosed volume would be present and \(\beta_2\) would be zero.
For example, a sphere surface has \((1,0,1)\), whereas a solid ball has \((1,0,0)\). A torus surface has \((1,2,1)\): the figure highlights its two independent loop directions. A solid torus has \((1,1,0)\). Filling its material removes the closed-surface class and the loop around the tube, but the central tunnel remains.

title: Foundation 2A: Homology counts holes
section: What can a hole mean in data?
text:
What can a hole mean in data?
The mathematics counts holes in the constructed space. Their scientific meaning comes from what that space represents:

In a sensor network, a one-dimensional class can indicate a region not covered by sensing neighbourhoods (Silva and Ghrist 2007).
In a sliding-window representation of a signal, a strong one-dimensional class can express periodic recurrence rather than an empty region in physical space (Perea and Harer 2015).
In grid-cell population activity, the pattern \((\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)=(1,2,1)\) supported a toroidal latent state space (Gardner et al. 2022).
In a reconstructed neocortical network, directed flag complexes encoded the direction of synaptic transmission. Their cavities supplied a global description of information-flow organisation and were related to stimulus-evoked activity (Reimann et al. 2017).
In collective-motion models, components and loops can describe clustering, fragmentation and occupation of a periodic spatial domain (Topaz et al. 2015).

These examples do not give a universal dictionary. A one-dimensional class is only “recurrence”, “uncovered territory” or “circulation” when the data, representation and construction justify that interpretation.


Beyond spatial holes. In a high-dimensional state, feature or relational space, a hole need not surround a literal empty region that could be drawn in physical space. The algebraic question remains the same: is a closed \(p\)-dimensional structure the boundary of an available \((p+1)\)-dimensional structure?

You are ready to continue when you can identify 0-, 1- and 2-dimensional holes in the classical spaces, read their Betti numbers, and explain why the meaning of a hole depends on the represented object.

title: Foundation 1B: Simplicial complexes in detail
text:
These building blocks have a common name. A vertex is a 0-simplex, an edge is a 1-simplex, and a filled triangle is a 2-simplex. More generally, an abstract \(p\)-simplex is a set of \(p+1\) vertices,
\[
\sigma=[v_0,\ldots,v_p].
\]
Its dimension is \(\dim\sigma=p\). A face is any simplex obtained from a subset of these vertices. A codimension-one face removes exactly one vertex.


Why “codimension”? The codimension of a face inside a simplex is the difference between their dimensions. Removing one vertex lowers the dimension by one, so the resulting face has codimension one.
A finite abstract simplicial complex on a vertex set \(V\) is a collection \(K\) of non-empty finite subsets of \(V\) such that
\[
\sigma\in K,\quad \varnothing\ne\tau\subseteq\sigma
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau\in K.
\]


What is required of \(K\)? For the abstract complexes used here, downward closure is the defining compatibility condition. Finiteness is a separate assumption that keeps the course calculations and software finite. A geometrically embedded simplicial complex must also satisfy geometric intersection conditions, but its abstract incidence structure is still downward closed.
The dimension of \(K\) is the largest dimension of any simplex in \(K\). The condition above is downward closure: whenever a simplex belongs to \(K\), all of its faces must belong to \(K\) as well. A filled triangle therefore brings its three edges and three vertices with it.


Why downward closure? Homology will take the boundary of each simplex. Its faces must already be simplices of \(K\), otherwise the boundary map would leave the vector spaces built from \(K\). Filtrations later require every stage to be a valid complex, but tracking birth and death is not the reason for imposing this rule.
For example,
\[
\{[v_0],[v_1],[v_2],[v_0,v_1],[v_1,v_2],[v_0,v_2],[v_0,v_1,v_2]\}
\]
is a simplicial complex. The collection
\[
\{[v_0],[v_1],[v_2],[v_0,v_1,v_2]\}
\]
is not, because it contains a triangle while omitting its edges.


Graph, hypergraph or simplicial complex? A graph records pairwise relations. A hypergraph may record a five-person interaction without asserting that every pair interacted. A simplicial complex includes every lower-order face, so turning that hyperedge into a simplex adds all subgroup relations. That is a modelling decision, not merely a change of notation.

A subcomplex \(L\subseteq K\) is a collection of simplices from \(K\) that is itself downward closed. The inclusion
\[
\iota:L\hookrightarrow K
\]
sends each simplex of \(L\) to that same simplex in \(K\).


Reading \(L\hookrightarrow K\). The hooked arrow signals inclusion. Here \(K\) is larger only as a collection of simplices: it contains everything in \(L\), and possibly more. A subcomplex really is a subset, but a special one; an arbitrary subset of the simplices of \(K\) may fail downward closure.
The \(p\)-skeleton \(K^{(p)}\) contains every simplex of dimension at most \(p\). In particular, \(K^{(1)}\) is the graph formed by the vertices and edges. It omits filled triangles and every higher-dimensional simplex.

For a graph \(G\), the clique complex \(\mathrm{Cl}(G)\), also called its flag complex, contains one simplex for every complete subgraph. Three mutually adjacent vertices produce a 2-simplex; four produce a 3-simplex together with all of its faces. Thus a graph and its clique complex have the same vertices and edges but need not have the same first homology.


Flag or clique? The terms are interchangeable. Flag complex is common in topology and algebra, while clique complex is common in combinatorics and network science.

Assigning locations to vertices and drawing their convex hulls gives a geometric realisation. The abstract incidence information, not the coordinates of one drawing, defines the complex. The notation \(|K|\) denotes the space obtained by gluing geometric simplices according to those incidences. When \(|K|\) represents a continuous space, \(K\) is a triangulation of that space.


ExampleThe house complex


The labelled house combines two edge cycles with one filled triangular face.



The labelled house simplicial complex.


Its vertices are \(v_0,\ldots,v_4\). Its six edges are
\[
x=[v_0,v_1],\quad y=[v_1,v_2],\quad z=[v_2,v_3],
\]
\[
u=[v_3,v_4],\quad v=[v_4,v_0],\quad w=[v_4,v_1],
\]
and its only 2-simplex is the filled roof \(t=[v_0,v_1,v_4]\). Downward closure supplies the edges and vertices of \(t\).
The 1-skeleton contains two visible edge cycles, the roof and the room. The full complex also contains \(t\), so the roof cycle is filled while the room cycle is not. This distinction is what the homology calculation must detect.



You are ready to continue when you can read the formal downward-closure rule, form a subcomplex, identify a skeleton and explain what clique filling adds to a graph.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
A set is a collection of elements. If \(x\) is an element of \(X\), write \(x\in X\). If every element of \(U\) belongs to \(X\), write \(U\subseteq X\). The empty set \(\varnothing\) has no elements.
When a set is treated as a space, its elements are called points. “Point” and “element” refer to the same member of the set; the word point signals that spatial structure matters.






NoteExample: elements, subsets and collections





For \(X=\{a,b,c\}\), the statement \(a\in X\) concerns an element, while \(\{a,b\}\subseteq X\) concerns a subset. A collection such as \(\mathcal T=\{\varnothing,\{a\},X\}\) has subsets of \(X\) as its elements.

When a set is treated as a space, its elements are called points. “Point” and “element” refer to the same member of the set; the word point signals that spatial structure matters.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Open sets and topology
An open set is a subset declared to contain some neighbourhood around each of its points. The precise declaration is supplied by a topology.
A topology on \(X\) is a collection \(\mathcal T\) of subsets of \(X\) such that:

\(\varnothing\) and \(X\) belong to \(\mathcal T\);
any union of members of \(\mathcal T\) belongs to \(\mathcal T\); and
any finite intersection of members of \(\mathcal T\) belongs to \(\mathcal T\).

The pair \((X,\mathcal T)\) is a topological space, and the members of \(\mathcal T\) are its open sets.
In ordinary language, the rules ensure that the whole space is available as a neighbourhood, open regions can be joined, and finitely many open conditions can be imposed simultaneously without losing openness.






NoteExample: a topology on three points





Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) and
\[
\mathcal T=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{a,b\},X\}.
\]
The required empty and whole sets are present. Unions and finite intersections of listed sets remain listed, so \(\mathcal T\) is a topology. The subset \(\{b\}\) is not open in this topology.



Open is not an intrinsic property of a subset. The same set \(X\) can carry different topologies, representing different notions of neighbourhood.


Intuition. A topology specifies which local distinctions the space allows us to make continuously. More open sets mean a finer ability to distinguish neighbourhoods.

Why intersections are only required to be finite
Finite intersections preserve a positive amount of neighbourhood room. Infinite intersections may shrink that room to nothing. For example,
\[
\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1/n,1/n)=\{0\},
\]
and the singleton \(\{0\}\) is not open in the usual topology on \(\mathbb R\).

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Metrics and open balls
A metric is a distance function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying:

\(d(x,y)\geq0\), with \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\);
\(d(x,y)=d(y,x)\); and
\(d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)\).

The second part of the first rule is sometimes called identity of indiscernibles: distinct points must not have zero distance.
The open ball of radius \(r>0\) around \(x\) is
\[
B_r(x)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}.
\]
A subset is open in the metric topology when every one of its points lies in some ball contained within the subset.



Different metrics produce differently shaped open balls.


Different metrics produce different balls and different notions of proximity. Euclidean balls are circular in two dimensions; Manhattan-distance balls are diamond-shaped. Weighting one coordinate more heavily produces ellipses in the original coordinates.


Dynamical and complex systems intuition. Weighting a direction can encode unequal units or anisotropic dynamics. It changes which state differences are treated as small.

Data analysis intuition. Scaling variables changes distances and hence neighbourhoods. Standardisation is a modelling choice when proximity drives the analysis.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Continuity
A map \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous if the preimage of every open set in \(Y\) is open in \(X\):
\[
V\text{ open in }Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^{-1}(V)\text{ open in }X.
\]
Intuitively, nearby output requirements pull back to neighbourhood requirements in the input. The map has no abrupt tear in the topology being used.


Dynamical and complex systems intuition. Continuous finite-time evolution can amplify small differences without making instantaneous jumps. Continuity and stability are not the same claim.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Connectedness and paths
A space is connected if it cannot be separated into two disjoint, non-empty open subsets. It is path-connected if any two points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the space.
Path-connectedness implies connectedness. For the familiar spaces and finite complexes used here, thinking in terms of continuous paths gives the intended intuition.






NoteExample: one piece or two





The interval \([0,1]\) is path-connected. The union \([0,1]\cup[2,3]\) has two connected components because the gap prevents any path within the space from joining the intervals.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Homeomorphism: the same topology
A homeomorphism is a bijection \(f:X\to Y\) for which both \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are continuous. Spaces related by such a map are homeomorphic.
The rubber sheet metaphor describes this informally. A space may be stretched, bent or twisted, but not cut, glued or irreversibly collapsed. Requiring the inverse to be continuous makes the deformation reversible.






NoteExample: circle, ellipse and segment





A circle and ellipse are homeomorphic. A circle and line segment are not: removing an interior point disconnects the segment, while removing one point from a circle leaves one connected arc.



The cup-and-doughnut slogan applies only after the spaces are specified. The solid material, boundary surface, liquid-containing region and a finite scan are different mathematical objects. A hollow handle may also change the selected space.


Caution. A continuous map alone need not preserve topology. A constant map is continuous but collapses an entire space to one point.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Homotopy and deformation retracts
A homotopy is a continuous deformation from one map to another. Two spaces are homotopy equivalent when maps between them compose to maps homotopic to the corresponding identity maps. This is weaker than homeomorphism.
A space is contractible when it is homotopy equivalent to a point. A filled disc is contractible even though it is not homeomorphic to a point.
A deformation retract continuously contracts a space onto a subspace while keeping that subspace fixed. An annulus deformation retracts onto its central circle: radial thickness is discarded, but the loop remains.


Intuition. A deformation retract identifies structure that can be removed without changing the essential loop organisation. It is a controlled collapse, not a homeomorphism.
Homotopic describes maps with the same domain and codomain. Homotopy equivalent describes spaces related by suitable maps in both directions.

title: Prelude B: Topology in detail
text:
Homology: a computable invariant
Homology assigns algebraic objects \(H_p(X)\) to a space. Informally, \(H_0\) records components, \(H_1\) records independent loop classes and \(H_2\) records independent closed-surface classes.
Homotopy-equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology:
\[
X\simeq Y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H_p(X)\cong H_p(Y).
\]
The converse need not hold. Homology deliberately forgets some information about how loops and higher-dimensional structures interact.






NoteExample: outline and filling





An outline triangle realises a circle and has one \(H_1\) class. Adding its triangular face supplies a filling, so the resulting disc has \(H_1=0\).



There is no standard relation called “homologic” analogous to “homotopic”. We say that two spaces have isomorphic homology groups, or more informally that they have the same homology over stated coefficients.

title: Practical notebooks and software scope
text:
Current software scope
Python is the course’s primary environment because it provides a coherent route through numerical work, plotting, point-cloud persistence, simplex-tree representations and cubical complexes. The notebooks expose small constructions directly before using Ripser.py, Persim or GUDHI.
Julia is a planned research extension, particularly when a surrounding dynamical simulation is Julia-native or a Ripserer.jl benchmark becomes scientifically useful. A mixed-language workflow should exchange simple objects such as point arrays, distance matrices or persistence intervals rather than live complex objects.
The supported teaching workflow covers ordinary persistence, diagram comparison, vectorisation and snapshot persistence. Zigzag, multiparameter and vineyard-module computation require separate specialist evaluation; ordinary Ripser interoperability does not supply those methods automatically.

text:
Create the course environment
The environment file specifies Python 3.11 and the packages used across the course, including NumPy, Matplotlib, GUDHI, Ripser, Persim and Dionysus. Dionysus is used only in the optional vineyard extension within Topic 6.

Why the course currently uses Python
All practical notebooks are currently written in Python. Python gives the mixed course audience a widely used notebook environment and a mature collection of interoperable tools for numerical work, plotting and TDA. Using one language also lets the course concentrate on mathematical constructions and modelling decisions instead of maintaining two parallel implementations.
Julia is an intended future extension, especially for dynamical systems workflows and research-scale numerical experiments. The plan is to add Julia translations after the Python notebooks and their outputs are stable and tested. Until then, Python is the supported teaching route rather than an endorsement that TDA must be done in Python.

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate tda-masterclass
jupyter lab

conda env update -f environment.yml --prune

title: Topological Data Analysis for the Complex Systems Scientist
text:
This MasterClass is a documented route into topological data analysis for a complex systems scientist, applied mathematician or data analyst who may not have an algebraic topology background but wants more than a surface-level introduction. It may also be useful to students meeting these ideas for the first time.
The goal is conceptual fluency: to understand what a persistent homology pipeline constructs, follow the argument in a technical paper, and recognise where scientific judgement enters. Running a TDA package is relatively easy. The harder part is knowing what was constructed, which choices produced it and what the result means. The computations here make those steps visible.
The question running through the material is:
No prior algebraic topology is assumed. The formal topology refresher and algebra refresher are references to consult when a definition or calculation needs unpacking.
Accompanying notebooks. Each stage has a downloadable Python notebook. The supplied example rebuilds the main object or figure from the reader, while short exercises expose the choices inside the calculation. The data input is kept separate so that the same calculation can be tested on another data set.

title: Topological Data Analysis for the Complex Systems Scientist
text:
The persistent homology construction
By the end of the foundation material, every object and map in this construction should be clear. It is the guiding framework for everything that follows. The numbered margin notes link each part to its intuitive and formal development.

Let \(K\) be a finite simplicial complex.


1 · Build \(K\). Turn the data and modelling choices into a finite representation. Why a representation is needed and simplicial complexes in detail.
For a coefficient field \(\mathbb F\), \(H_p(K;\mathbb F)\) records its \(p\)-dimensional homology.


2 · Homology of \(K\). Calculate the homology of that representation. What homology records and chains and boundary maps.
Let
\[
f:K\to\mathbb R
\]
be monotone on faces, meaning \(f(\sigma)\leq f(\tau)\) whenever \(\sigma\) is a face of \(\tau\). The sublevel complexes
\[
K_a=\{\sigma\in K:f(\sigma)\leq a\}
\]
form a filtration: \(K_a\subseteq K_b\) whenever \(a\leq b\). Write \(\iota_{a,b}:K_a\hookrightarrow K_b\) for this inclusion, and use \(\mathcal K_f\) as shorthand for the entire indexed filtration and its inclusions.


3 · Filter \(K\). Repeat the construction through a nested family. Why filtrations are needed and filtrations in detail.
Applying homology gives vector spaces and induced maps
\[
V_a=H_p(K_a;\mathbb F),
\qquad
\phi_{a,b}=H_p(\iota_{a,b}):V_a\to V_b.
\]
They satisfy
\[
\phi_{a,a}=\operatorname{id}_{V_a},
\qquad
\phi_{b,c}\circ\phi_{a,b}=\phi_{a,c}.
\]
The functor \(V=H_p\circ\mathcal K_f\), equivalently the family \(\{V_a,\phi_{a,b}\}_{a\leq b}\), is the degree-\(p\) persistence module. For a particular pair \(a\leq b\), the persistent homology group from \(a\) to \(b\) is
\[
H_p^{a,b}=\operatorname{im}\phi_{a,b}.
\]
It contains the classes present by scale \(a\) that remain alive at scale \(b\).


4 · Persistent homology. Retain the maps that say what survives across the family. Follow classes across scale and persistence modules in detail.
For a finite one-parameter filtration over a field, the persistence module admits an interval decomposition. The same intervals are displayed as a barcode or persistence diagram:
\[
V\cong\bigoplus_{\ell}I_{[b_\ell,d_\ell)}
\qquad
\operatorname{Bar}_p(V),\ \operatorname{Dgm}_p(V).
\]


5 · Encode the module. Record the resulting lifespans as bars or birth-death points. Barcodes and diagrams and decomposition and reduction.
The data, preprocessing, metric or relation, and the choices of \(K\) and \(f\) all precede the algebra and remain part of the scientific model.

title: Applied glossary
text:
Mathematical term
Precise meaning
Applied or intuitive translation
Interpretation caution




Set
A collection of elements.
The collection of items currently being treated as one mathematical object.
A set alone carries no distance, neighbourhood or continuity structure.


Point
An element of a set when that set is being treated as a space.
One possible location, state or observation in the represented space.
“Point” describes its role in the space, not necessarily a literal spatial dot.


Open set
A member of the topology; in a metric space, every included point has a sufficiently small ball contained in the set.
A region that leaves local room around each of its points.
Openness belongs to the chosen topology, not to a subset in isolation.


Topology
A collection of subsets containing the empty set and whole space and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
The declared neighbourhood structure that makes continuity meaningful.
It is not a generic synonym for shape.


Topological space
A set equipped with open sets satisfying the topology axioms.
A specification of which points count as locally near one another, without requiring numerical distance.
“Topology” is not a generic synonym for shape or network layout.


Continuous map
A map whose preimage of every open set is open.
A transformation that does not introduce abrupt topological breaks.
Continuity depends on the topologies on both domain and codomain.


Connected space
A space that cannot be separated into two disjoint non-empty open subsets.
One piece at the level of continuous organisation.
Connected does not always mean path-connected.


Homeomorphism
A bijection whose forward and inverse maps are continuous.
A reversible deformation that preserves topological structure.
The rubber sheet metaphor concerns continuous spaces. A bare finite sample is discrete, so a data analysis first needs a stated finite representation.


Homotopy equivalence
Maps in both directions whose composites are homotopic to the corresponding identity maps.
Two spaces retain the same broad continuous shape after contractible detail is ignored.
It is weaker than homeomorphism and does not preserve metric geometry.


Homotopy
A continuous deformation from one map to another.
A continuously varying family of transformations.
Homotopy relates maps; homotopy equivalence of spaces requires maps in both directions with suitable composites.


Contractible space
A space homotopy equivalent to a point.
A space whose topological structure can be continuously collapsed away.
Contractible does not mean geometrically small.


Deformation retract
A continuous deformation of a space onto a subspace that keeps every point of the subspace fixed.
Collapse dispensable material while leaving a chosen structural core unmoved.
The retract must remain inside the original space throughout the deformation.


Path-connected
Every pair of points can be joined by a continuous path lying in the space.
Any location can be reached continuously from any other without leaving the object.
Path-connectedness implies connectedness, but the converse can fail for unusual spaces.


Topological invariant
A quantity or algebraic object unchanged under homeomorphism.
A shape descriptor designed to ignore coordinates and reversible deformation.
In data analysis it is computed on a constructed representation, not directly on an unknown physical system.


Constructed representation
A mathematical object built from observations and modelling choices.
The point cloud, graph, image complex or embedding through which the system is analysed.
It can amplify, erase or invent apparent organisation relative to the scientific object.


Metric
A distance function satisfying non-negativity, identity, symmetry and the triangle inequality.
The rule that decides which observations are similar enough to interact first.
A convenient metric may be scientifically inappropriate.


Point cloud
A finite subset of a metric space.
A collection of sampled states or observations represented as points.
It is a representation of the system, not automatically the system or attractor itself.


Geometric descriptor
A quantity or representation measuring a specified metric or coordinate property of a geometric object.
One deliberately chosen answer to “what makes these shapes look different?”, such as spacing, area, direction or curvature.
No short list of descriptors is a complete definition of shape; inspect what each retains and discards.


Convex hull
The smallest convex set containing a specified set of points.
A tight elastic band placed around the outermost observations.
It records the outer envelope but cannot detect internal gaps, density or concavity.


Anisotropy
Dependence of measured properties on direction.
Evidence that a cloud stretches or organises more strongly along some directions than others.
A single anisotropy ratio can miss curvature, multiple branches and local changes in direction.


Geometric simplex
The convex hull of affinely independent vertices.
A filled-in building block: point, segment, triangle, tetrahedron.
A drawn triangle and three edges do not specify whether the face is filled.


Abstract simplex
A finite set of vertices.
A recorded multiway relation among the listed vertices.
It need not have physical extent or a unique embedding.


Vertex
A 0-simplex and basic element from which higher simplices are formed.
One observation, state, agent or other basic item in the representation.
A plotted location is a geometric placement of the vertex, not the abstract vertex itself.


Edge
A 1-simplex containing two vertices.
A declaration that two represented items count as related.
The scientific meaning of the relation comes from the construction.


Filled triangle
A 2-simplex containing three vertices and all of its faces.
A coherent three-way relation or filled patch rather than an empty three-edge loop.
Three pairwise edges do not by themselves force a filled triangle unless the construction says so.


Simplex dimension
A \(p\)-simplex has \(p+1\) vertices; vertices, edges and filled triangles are 0-, 1- and 2-simplices.
The dimension names the order of the filled building block.
A 2-simplex is filled; a triangular outline contains only 0- and 1-simplices.


Simplicial complex
A collection of simplices closed under taking faces.
A consistent catalogue of relations at every included order.
Its 1-skeleton does not determine its higher-dimensional simplices.


Downward closure
Every non-empty face of an included simplex must also belong to the complex.
A group relation brings all of its required lower-order pieces with it.
This condition distinguishes a simplicial complex from a general hypergraph.


Geometric realisation \(|K|\)
A topological space obtained by realising and gluing the simplices of \(K\).
A spatial version of the abstract incidence data.
The realisation is not necessarily the observed physical object.


1-skeleton
All vertices and edges of a complex.
The network visible after discarding filled triangles and higher relations.
Homology of the graph may differ from homology of the full complex.


Subcomplex
A downward-closed subset of the simplices of a complex.
A smaller valid complex contained within a larger one.
An arbitrary selection of simplices need not be a subcomplex.


Clique complex
The complex containing a simplex for every clique of a graph.
Treat every mutually pairwise-connected group as one higher-order unit.
Clique filling is a modelling assumption about higher-order coherence.


Cubical complex
A complex built from vertices, edges, pixels, voxels and higher-dimensional cubes.
A topology-ready representation of gridded images, fields or volumes.
Cell-value conventions and filtration direction determine what birth means.


Triangulation
A simplicial complex whose geometric realisation represents a given topological space.
A finite assembly of simplices used to model the continuous object.
Different triangulations can represent the same space.


Graph cycle rank
For a finite undirected graph, \(E-V+C\), the dimension of its cycle space over a field.
The number of independent network loops before any higher-dimensional filling is added.
It is not generally \(H_1\) of the clique complex because triangles and higher simplices can fill graph cycles.
